extracted.subtask_description: Apply Tolstoy's aesthetic theory to judge whether a work of fiction genuinely transmits the author's feeling to readers, focusing on individuality, clarity, sincerity, universality, and inner necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infectiousness (transmission of feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: "To evoke in oneself a feeling one has once experienced, and having evoked it in oneself then by means of movements, lines, colors, sounds, or forms expressed in words, so to transmit that feeling that others may experience the same feeling — this is the activity of art." Art = the infection of one mind by another with a feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary test of art is whether the artist's feeling is transmitted such that others experience the same feeling. The medium (words, sounds, colors, etc.) is instrumental; the core is that feeling crosses from artist to receiver. Evaluate works by asking: did I catch the same feeling the artist had?

rubrics_metrics.name: Individuality of Feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more individual the feeling transmitted the more strongly does it act on the receiver; the more individual the state of soul into which he is transferred the more pleasure does the receiver obtain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particular, distinctive, personal feelings produce strong infection; generic, formulaic, common feelings produce weak infection. The cliché is the enemy of infection. Look for feelings that feel unique to the artist's experience rather than stock emotional formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness of Transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: "The receiver... is the better satisfied the more clearly the feeling is transmitted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confused, garbled, or occluded expression weakens the infectiousness of art. Clarity is not opposed to depth—lucidity helps carry the feeling intact to the reader. Assess whether the expression communicates the intended feeling cleanly without unnecessary obfuscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity of the Artist
rubrics_metrics.description: "The degree of infectiousness of art is increased most of all by the degree of sincerity in the artist. As soon as the spectator feels that the artist is infected by his own production... this mental condition of the artist infects the receiver."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sincerity — the artist truly feeling what they express rather than simulating it for effect — is central. Readers can sense performance versus genuine feeling; the former produces weak or counterfeit infection. Sincerity increases infectiousness and is prioritized above other virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner Necessity (work proceeds from inner need)
rubrics_metrics.description: The genuinely sincere artist works from inner necessity; the work springs from the artist's inner need rather than from external motives or calculated effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a work is created from inner necessity it is likelier to transmit a particular feeling and to seek the clarity needed for infection. Anti-patterns include writing primarily for fame, market, imitation, or technical display rather than from inward compulsion — such motives weaken infectiousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universality (moral purpose: shared feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Tolstoy, art's purpose is moral: to unite human beings in shared feeling. Good art is universal in its emotional accessibility while local in its specific feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the transmitted feeling can cross persons, eras, and cultures (is emotionally accessible to others) while remaining a particular, lived feeling. Works that divide, appeal only to elites, or are sensual without creating communion are judged 'bad' in this frame. Tolstoy's moral-religious stance informs controversial value judgments (e.g., dismissing celebrated works that fail universality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative criterion: not a work of art if conditions fail
rubrics_metrics.description: A work that (1) fails to transmit the artist's peculiar feeling (not individual), (2) is unintelligibly expressed (not clear), or (3) did not proceed from inner need (not sincere) is 'not a work of art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a strong exclusionary claim: failing any of these central conditions disqualifies a piece from being art in Tolstoy's terms. Use this as a decisive anti-pattern when a work feels formulaic, opaque, or merely performative; note that many critically praised works may still fail this test according to Tolstoy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical evaluative checklist (Tolstoy's summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess fiction on: Individuality — does the feeling transmitted feel like nobody else's? Clarity — does it land cleanly, without occlusion? Sincerity — does the writer actually feel this, or perform feeling it? Universality — can the feeling cross persons (reader, era, culture)? Inner necessity — was this written from need, or for effect?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these five interrelated items as a compact rubric for judging whether a story 'infects' the reader. Tolstoy emphasizes that sincerity tends to produce individuality and clarity; the highest-rated works pass all five but are rare.
